header:
Date: 2026-09-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Arjun Mehta (Redwood CSM) -- Liam O'Rourke (Mercator CTO), Sana Park (ML Eng), Diego Ramos (SRE), Hannah Li (PM)
summary: Discovery to map Mercator's escape path from current vLLM/TGI self-hosted stack to Redwood's hosted/dedicated/private offerings. Main themes: parity (quality & features), latency vs cost tradeoffs, KV cache and streaming behavior, SSO/KMS/security controls, practical pilot scope and timelines.
topics: Hosting options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, um we've got about 45 minutes so i'll jump in — quick intros from the redwood side then we'll hear where you are.
[00:07] Liam: yes thanks, liam here CTO at Mercator, we run a mix of cloud-hosted and on-prem inference, primary concern is we need output parity with our current TGI/vLLM pipelines.
[00:15] Maya (SE): hi liam, maya from redwood, we do a lot of portouts from tgi/vllm — curious about your current model family and token lengths?
[00:22] Sana: we're on a mix: fine-tuned Llama-2 variants + a few smaller instruction-tuned open models for lower-cost endpoints. typical convo length ~ 700 tokens, sometimes spikes to 4k for analytics summarization.
[00:34] Diego: and for throughput we batch heavily, vllm gives us control but the ops overhead is non-trivial. we're probing if we can move to hosted or dedicated while keeping costs in line.
[00:44] Jordan: great context. two quick clarifying questions: 1) do you need data residency / air-gapped on day one? 2) what's your target latency p95 for interactive flows?
[00:52] Liam: not full air gap, but we do require EU residency for some customers and strict audit logs. latency target p95 is <300ms for small prompts, for the heavy 4k jobs it's more like we accept 800-1200ms.
[01:05] Maya: ok that maps well to redwood hosted for quick on-ramp and dedicated for consistent tail latencies — private on-prem is there when residency/audit/control is required.
[01:13] Hannah (PM): can you describe how you handle model upgrades / rollouts? we have a lot of tight SLAs for models used in-prod and are anxious about regression.
[01:20] Arjun (CSM): we have rollout primitives — canary, A/B, automatic fallback to previous model variants — and quality monitoring that can be tied to your eval prompt set so regressions trigger alerts.
[01:33] Sana: that sounds helpful. the big ask is that behavior matches our vLLM baseline — generation quirks, tokenization edge cases, system prompt handling — basically parity.
[01:42] Maya: totally. parity work is usually two parts: (1) a metrics/quality parity bench — embedding similarity, token-level diffs, heuristic checks for trailing/stop sequences; (2) perf parity — p95/p99 latency and cost per token. we typically run both with customer prompt sets.
[01:56] Liam: quick question around kv cache — in our current vLLM setup we keep a lightweight long-term KV to speed up multi-turn sessions, do you expose similar cache controls?
[02:04] Maya: yes we have prefix/KV caching semantics — you can configure cache TTL and we support hot-kv pinned per-session to reduce decode cost. behaviour can differ slightly across runtimes and we'll surface that in the bench.
[02:14] Diego: and quantization — we run int8 for many models, does redwood support quantized execution and do you preserve quality?
[02:20] Jordan: we have quantization-aware profiles, and our runtime chooses kernels that preserve output fidelity. for some very sensitive finetuned weights we recommend a light eval before switching to int8.
[02:30] Sana: okay, can we see an example of where outputs diverge? sometimes small tokenization or spacing differences break downstream parsers.
[02:38] Maya: yes we'll include token-diff examples in bench results and also produce a diff-triggered sample set for your QA.
[02:44] Liam: what about function/tool calling? we rely on structured JSON output for certain endpoints and a couple of models that do poor structured output.
[02:52] Maya: streaming + structured output support is in our hosted API; we also have tool-calling primitives that can be wired to your orchestration. some of the older open models need wrapper prompts to stabilize JSON, we'll include recommended prompt templates.
[03:06] Diego: how do you handle fallbacks? if a model variant is overloaded you're able to drain to a cheaper/compatible variant?
[03:12] Arjun: yes routing policies allow fallback to a compatible model, or to degrade to a lower-cost path while preserving minimal correctness. you can set policy to prefer latency or prefer cost.
[03:22] Hannah: security—SSO, SAML, RBAC and KMS are must-haves. also we need audit log retention controls for 12 months.
[03:30] Jordan: we support SSO/SAML, granular RBAC, KMS integrations (bring-your-own-key with HSM options) and configurable audit retention. we'll attach the security pack.
[03:39] Liam: network-wise if we go private we want a VPC peering option and control plane separation. whats the difference in effort between dedicated and private?
[03:47] Maya: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools hosted by redwood but controlled through the shared control plane — faster to provision. Private gives you a control plane that can be customer-managed and on-prem installers; provisioning takes longer (ops planning, infra hardening) and we'll run an install checklist together.
[04:03] Sana: are there customers who ran the parity bench in 48 hours? we need a quick signal before committing to a pilot.
[04:09] Maya: yes, we often do a 48–72 hour parity run with your prompt set and traffic shape. typically we surface a spreadsheet with token-level latency/cost breakdown and a small quality report.
[04:20] Liam: ok that timing works. what's involved in the bench setup? we run vLLM/TGI on prem, can you run Redwood hosted against a mirror of prompts?
[04:29] Maya: two options — we can run hosted vs your vllm benchmarks if you can provide prompts and expected checks, or we can spin a short-lived dedicated pool and run the bench from our side to match infra. the former is faster, the latter closer to production parity.
[04:42] Diego: we will need to share sample prompts and a small dataset — i'll put that in the action items. one more question: billing granularity — we need per-team cost breakdown and token-level attribution for chargeback.
[04:54] Arjun: console supports token-level breakdowns by API key/route and you can export CSVs for cost allocation.
[05:01] Liam: also curious about burst capacity — some nights we get a spike and our vllm fleet can accept bursts by adding ephemeral nodes. how fast can redwood scale?
[05:10] Jordan: Dedicated has configurable burst capacity and autoscaling policies; hosted offers transparent autoscaling with preemptive warm pools for common model families. we can model your traffic and propose burst sizing in the pricing draft.
[05:22] Sana: on fine-tunes — we have a couple of proprietary finetunes, can we bring those? are weights kept encrypted and is inference kept within our VPC if private?
[05:33] Maya: you can bring your own weights. for private deployments inference stays within your VPC and we support encrypted at-rest and in-transit, and BYOK so only you hold the unwrapped key. for hosted/dedicated we offer RBAC + KMS options and strict tenant isolation.
[05:48] Hannah: what's a realistic pilot? 6 weeks? 3 months?
[05:54] Jordan: typical pilot is 4–8 weeks: initial parity bench (48–72h), a small dedicated pool for week-long smoke tests, and then a pilot with limited traffic ramp and monitoring. timeline depends on private on-prem requirements.
[06:06] Liam: that's helpful. one risk we keep seeing is small functional regressions — generation formatting, prefer vs hallucinations — can redwood help with eval hooks?
[06:14] Maya: yep we integrate evals—attach your prompt set and we can run automated quality checks on every rollout and alert on regressions with sample traces.
[06:24] Diego: ok i'll share our vllm config (thread/worker counts, kv settings) plus a hygiene script.
[06:30] Jordan: perfect — to recap next steps: jordan will send pricing draft and security packet; maya will run the parity bench and share results; diego will send prompts and configs. we'll target a follow-up to review bench results.
[06:42] Liam: thanks, appreciate the practical approach — we'll aim to get you the dataset by friday.
[06:46] Arjun: thanks everyone, i'll book the follow-up for next wednesday tentatively.
[06:50] Speaker 1 (misc): mm-hmm okay great thanks bye.
[06:53] END OF TRANSCRIPT
